questions.q: If z = 2 − 3i, what is z² − 4z?
a and b are elements of a group. Which expression is always equal to (ab)⁻¹?
questions.x: (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹) = a(bb⁻¹)a⁻¹ = aa⁻¹ = e, so (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹: the order reverses. a⁻¹b⁻¹ is equal to it only in a commutative group.

questions.q: What is the range of f(x) = √(4 − x²)?
questions.x: The domain is −2 ≤ x ≤ 2, where 4 − x² runs from 0 to 4, so its square root runs from 0 to 2. The range is [0, 2]; [−2, 2] is the domain.

questions.q: The graphs of y = log₂x and y = 3 − x meet at exactly one point. What is its x-coordinate?
questions.x: At x = 2, log₂2 = 1 and 3 − 2 = 1, so the graphs meet there. log₂x is increasing and 3 − x is decreasing, so they meet only once. At x = 1 the values are 0 and 2; at x = 4 they are 2 and −1.

questions.q: f(x) = 1/(x − 1) and g(x) = 1/(x + 2). At which points is the composite function f(g(x)) discontinuous?
questions.x: f(g(x)) is undefined where g is undefined (x = −2) and where g(x) = 1, i.e. x + 2 = 1, x = −1. Elsewhere it equals (x + 2)/(−x − 1), a continuous rational function. Using f's own break at x = 1 is the slip.

questions.q: A = [[1, 0, 2], [0, 3, 0], [1, 0, 1]]. What is the entry in row 1, column 3 of adj A?
questions.x: adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, so its (1, 3) entry is the cofactor C₃₁ = (+1)·|[[0, 2], [3, 0]]| = −6. Taking C₁₃ = |[[0, 3], [1, 0]]| = −3 forgets the transpose. Check: row 3 of A times column 3 of adj A is 1(−6) + 0 + 1(3) = −3 = |A|.

questions.q: A stone is thrown upward. Its height after t seconds is h = 20t − 5t² metres. For how many seconds is it at least 15 m above the ground?
questions.x: 20t − 5t² ≥ 15 gives t² − 4t + 3 ≤ 0, i.e. (t − 1)(t − 3) ≤ 0, so 1 ≤ t ≤ 3. That is 3 − 1 = 2 seconds. Check: h(1) = h(3) = 15 and h(2) = 20. Giving the later time 3 s instead of the length of the interval is the usual slip.

questions.q: How many integers x satisfy both x² < 3x + 10 and x² > 4?
questions.x: x² − 3x − 10 < 0 gives −2 < x < 5; x² > 4 gives x < −2 or x > 2. Together 2 < x < 5, so x = 3 or 4: two integers. Check x = −1: 1 > 4 fails. Using only the first inequality gives the six integers −1 to 4.

questions.q: Which single fraction equals 2/(x − 3) − 1/(x + 2)?
For which positive integer n is 1² + 2² + … + n² equal to 5 times 1 + 2 + … + n?
A box holds 4 red and 6 blue pens. In how many ways can 3 pens be chosen with at most one red pen?
questions.x: No red: C(6, 3) = 20. Exactly one red: 4 × C(6, 2) = 4 × 15 = 60. Total 80. Check: C(10, 3) = 120, minus two red (6 × 6 = 36) and three red (4) gives 80. 60 counts only the one-red case.

questions.q: Using the binomial theorem, the value of (0.99)⁵ correct to four decimal places is:
For |x| < 1/2, the first three terms of the expansion of (1 + 2x)⁻¹ are:
questions.x: (1 + y)⁻¹ = 1 − y + y² − … with y = 2x gives 1 − 2x + 4x². Writing y² as 2x² instead of (2x)² gives the 2x² slip.

questions.q: For every θ, sin(45° + θ) − cos(45° − θ) equals:
questions.x: sin(45° + θ) = (√2/2)(cos θ + sin θ) and cos(45° − θ) = (√2/2)(cos θ + sin θ), so the difference is 0. The two angles add to 90°, so the sine of one is the cosine of the other.

questions.q: A, B and C are the angles of a triangle (A + B + C = π). Which expression equals cos A + cos B + cos C?
questions.x: cos A + cos B = 2 sin(C/2) cos((A − B)/2) and cos C = 1 − 2 sin²(C/2); then cos((A − B)/2) − cos((A + B)/2) = 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) gives 1 + 4 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2). Check an equilateral triangle: 3/2 = 1 + 4 × 1/8. 4 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) cos(C/2) is sin A + sin B + sin C.

questions.q: What is the least value of y = 4 sin²x + 9 cosec²x (sin x ≠ 0)?
questions.x: With t = sin²x ∈ (0, 1], y = 4t + 9/t. AM–GM would give 12 at t = 3/2, but t cannot exceed 1. On (0, 1] y decreases, so the least value is at t = 1: 4 + 9 = 13.

questions.q: In any triangle ABC, a(b cos C − c cos B) equals:
questions.x: b cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2a) and c cos B = (a² + c² − b²)/(2a), so their difference is (b² − c²)/a; multiplying by a gives b² − c². It is 0 only when b = c, and b cos C + c cos B would give a.

questions.q: If cos⁻¹x = 2 sin⁻¹x, then x equals:
questions.x: Write cos⁻¹x = π/2 − sin⁻¹x, so π/2 = 3 sin⁻¹x and sin⁻¹x = π/6, giving x = 1/2. Check: cos⁻¹(1/2) = π/3 and 2 sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/3.

questions.q: The solutions of 2 sin θ tan θ = 3 in the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π are:
questions.x: 2 sin²θ/cos θ = 3 gives 2(1 − cos²θ) = 3 cos θ, i.e. 2cos²θ + 3cos θ − 2 = 0, (2cos θ − 1)(cos θ + 2) = 0, so cos θ = 1/2: θ = π/3, 5π/3. Check 5π/3: 2(−√3/2)(−√3) = 3.

questions.q: Using the Maclaurin series of ln(1 + x), what is lim(x→0) [ln(1 + x) − x]/x²?
questions.x: ln(1 + x) − x = −x²/2 + x³/3 − ..., so dividing by x² gives −1/2 + x/3 − ... → −1/2. Dropping the alternating sign gives 1/2.

questions.q: In the Maclaurin series of cos x, what is the coefficient of x³?
questions.x: cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − ...: only even powers appear, because the odd derivatives of cos x (−sin x, sin x, ...) are 0 at x = 0. −1/6 is the x³ coefficient of sin x.

questions.q: ∫ dx/(eˣ + 1) equals:
questions.x: Divide above and below by eˣ: ∫e^(−x)/(1 + e^(−x)) dx. With u = 1 + e^(−x), du = −e^(−x) dx, giving −ln(1 + e^(−x)) + C, which equals x − ln(1 + eˣ) + C. ln(1 + eˣ) has derivative eˣ/(1 + eˣ), not 1/(eˣ + 1).

questions.q: ∫ dx/(√(x + 1) − √x), for x > 0, equals:
questions.x: Multiply above and below by √(x + 1) + √x: the denominator becomes (x + 1) − x = 1, so the integrand is √(x + 1) + √x. Integrating gives (2/3)(x + 1)^(3/2) + (2/3)x^(3/2) + C.

questions.q: If dy/dx = y tan x and y = 2 when x = 0, what is y when x = π/3?
questions.x: Separate: dy/y = tan x dx, so ln y = −ln cos x + c, i.e. y = C sec x. y(0) = 2 gives C = 2, so y(π/3) = 2 × 2 = 4. Writing y = C cos x gives 1.

questions.q: One of the lines represented by 3x² + kxy − y² = 0 is y = 2x. What is the other line?
questions.x: Put y = 2x: 3 + 2k − 4 = 0, so k = ½. The product of the slopes is a/b = 3/(−1) = −3, so the other slope is −3/2: 3x + 2y = 0. Check: (2x − y)(3x + 2y) = 6x² + xy − 2y², twice the equation.

questions.q: What is the acute angle between the lines y = √3x and y = x/√3?
questions.x: Their inclinations are 60° and 30°, so the angle between them is 30°. Check: tan θ = |(√3 − 1/√3)/(1 + 1)| = (2/√3)/2 = 1/√3.

questions.q: Which point lies inside the ellipse x²/16 + y²/9 = 1?
questions.x: Inside means x²/16 + y²/9 < 1. (2, 2): 1/4 + 4/9 = 25/36 < 1. (3, 2): 9/16 + 4/9 = 145/144 > 1, just outside; (4, 1) is outside and (0, 3) is on the ellipse.

questions.q: For which values of k does x²/(k − 2) + y²/(k − 5) = 1 represent a hyperbola?
questions.x: A hyperbola needs the two denominators to have opposite signs: (k − 2)(k − 5) < 0, so 2 < k < 5. For k > 5 both are positive and the curve is an ellipse.

questions.q: Let a = i + j + k and b = i − j + k. Which vector is coplanar with a and b?
questions.x: 3i − j + 3k = a + 2b, so it lies in the plane of a and b. Check with triple products: [a, b, i] = 2, [a, b, j + k] = −2 and [a, b, k] = −2, none of them zero.

questions.q: The trapezium rule is used for ∫₁³ f(x) dx with h = 0.25. How many ordinates (function values) are needed?
questions.x: n = (3 − 1)/0.25 = 8 strips, which need n + 1 = 9 ordinates, y₀ to y₈. 8 counts the strips, not the ordinates.

questions.q: A light pulse travels 6 × 10⁴ m in 2 × 10⁻⁴ s. Its speed is:
questions.x: Speed = (6 × 10⁴)/(2 × 10⁻⁴) = 3 × 10⁴⁻⁽⁻⁴⁾ = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Adding the exponents instead of subtracting gives 3 × 10⁰; multiplying the numbers gives 1.2 × 10¹.

questions.q: For two non-zero vectors P and Q, the scalar product P · Q is equal to the magnitude of their vector product, |P × Q|. The angle between P and Q is:
questions.x: PQ cos θ = PQ sin θ gives tan θ = 1, so θ = 45°. At 90° the scalar product is zero, and at 0° the vector product is zero, so neither can be equal.

questions.q: The vector product of two parallel vectors is:
o: A scalar equal to the product of their magnitudes
questions.x: |P × Q| = PQ sin θ, and for parallel vectors θ = 0°, so sin θ = 0 and the product is the null vector. The maximum occurs at 90°; PQ is the scalar product for parallel vectors.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of a projectile's path the angle between its velocity and its acceleration is:
questions.x: At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal and the acceleration is g vertically downward, so they are at 90°. At launch the angle is greater than 90°; it is never 0° for a projectile launched at an angle.

questions.q: A body moves along a straight line with uniform velocity. Its velocity–time graph is:
o: A straight line sloping upward through the origin
questions.x: Uniform velocity means v does not change with time, so the graph is parallel to the time axis (zero slope, zero acceleration). A rising straight line describes uniform acceleration.

questions.q: A body is launched from the Earth's surface with exactly the escape velocity. Taking absolute potential energy as zero at infinity and ignoring air resistance, the total energy (kinetic plus potential) of the body is:
questions.x: At launch KE = ½mv² = GMm/R and PE = −GMm/R, so the total is zero, and it stays zero as the body just reaches infinity with zero speed. −GMm/2R is the total energy of a satellite in orbit at radius R, a bound state.

questions.q: A wheel turning at 12 rad s⁻¹ is slowed by a uniform angular retardation of 3 rad s⁻² until it stops. The angle it turns through while stopping is:
questions.x: ωf² = ωi² − 2αθ gives 0 = 144 − 6θ, so θ = 24 rad (check: it stops in 4 s at an average of 6 rad s⁻¹, 6 × 4 = 24 rad). Dropping the factor 2 gives 48 rad; 4 is the stopping time in seconds.

questions.q: A disc of radius 0.2 m has an angular acceleration of 15 rad s⁻². The tangential acceleration of a point on its rim is:
questions.x: a_t = rα = 0.2 × 15 = 3 m s⁻². Dividing α by r instead of multiplying gives 75 m s⁻².

questions.q: A mass hung from a spring stretches it by 25 cm at rest. It is then set into small vertical oscillations. A simple pendulum with the same time period has a length of:
questions.x: At rest mg = ke, so m/k = e/g and the spring's period is T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(e/g). A pendulum has T = 2π√(l/g), so l = e = 25 cm (both about 1 s).

questions.q: A particle performs SHM with a period of 0.5 s. Its angular frequency is:
questions.x: ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.5 = 4π rad s⁻¹ (check: f = 2 Hz, ω = 2πf = 4π). Multiplying 2π by T instead of dividing gives π rad s⁻¹.

questions.q: Beats are produced by the superposition of two sound waves that:
o: Have the same frequency and travel in opposite directions
Have the same frequency and are always in phase
Have very different frequencies and amplitudes
Have slightly different frequencies and travel in the same direction
questions.x: Two waves of slightly different frequency drift in and out of phase, so the loudness rises and falls: beats. Equal frequencies travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave instead.

questions.q: A polarimeter can be used to find the concentration of a sugar solution because the solution:
o: Rotates the plane of polarisation of light by an angle that depends on its concentration
Changes the wavelength of light in proportion to its concentration
Turns unpolarised light into plane-polarised light
questions.x: Sugar solution is optically active: it turns the plane of vibration of polarised light, and the angle of rotation grows with the concentration and the length of solution. The analyser is turned to measure that angle.

questions.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 500 nm, what is the path difference from the two slits to the centre of the third-order bright fringe (m = 3)?
questions.x: A bright fringe needs a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths: mλ = 3 × 500 = 1500 nm. The value 1250 nm (2.5λ) belongs to a dark fringe.

questions.q: A normal eye cannot see an object clearly when it is held closer than about 25 cm because:
o: The object then forms no image at all
The eye lens cannot be made any more converging to focus it
Light from close objects travels too slowly
questions.x: To focus nearer objects the eye muscles make the eye lens more converging (accommodation). At the near point the lens has reached its greatest power, so closer objects form a blurred image.

questions.q: For a monatomic ideal gas, Cv = 3R/2. Taking Cp − Cv = R, the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is:
questions.x: Cp = 3R/2 + R = 5R/2, so γ = (5R/2)/(3R/2) = 5/3. The value 7/5 is for a diatomic gas.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor is charged and then disconnected from the battery. Its plates are then pulled farther apart. Which statement is correct?
o: The charge and the potential difference both stay the same
The charge decreases and the energy decreases
The potential difference stays the same and the charge decreases
The charge stays the same, and the potential difference and stored energy both increase
questions.x: With the battery removed, Q cannot change. C = ε₀A/d falls, so V = Q/C rises and U = Q²/2C rises; the extra energy comes from the work done pulling the attracting plates apart.

questions.q: Two charges 10 cm apart in a medium of relative permittivity 4 exert a force F on each other. At what separation in vacuum would the same two charges exert the same force F?
questions.x: F = kq₁q₂/(εr r²), so the same force needs εr r² equal: 4 × 10² = r², giving r = 20 cm. Forgetting the square root gives 40 cm.

questions.q: In a metre bridge, resistor P is in the left gap and resistor Q in the right gap, and the balance point is 40 cm from the left end of the 100 cm wire. When a 5 Ω resistor is added in series with Q, the balance point moves to 30 cm from the left end. The value of P is:
questions.x: P/Q = 40/60, so P = 2Q/3. Then P/(Q + 5) = 30/70, so 7P = 3Q + 15; substituting, 14Q/3 = 3Q + 15, giving Q = 9 Ω and P = 6 Ω. Check: 6/14 = 3/7. 9 Ω is Q, not P.

questions.q: In a simple model of an atom, an electron moves round a circular orbit 5 × 10¹⁵ times per second. The equivalent current due to this motion is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):
questions.x: The charge e passes any point of the orbit f times per second, so I = ef = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5 × 10¹⁵ = 8 × 10⁻⁴ A. Dividing e by f instead of multiplying gives 3.2 × 10⁻³⁵ A.

questions.q: The total magnetic flux through any closed surface, for example a sphere drawn around a bar magnet, is:
o: Equal to the pole strength of the magnet
Largest when the magnet is at the centre of the sphere
Equal to B multiplied by the surface area
Zero, because magnetic field lines form closed loops
questions.x: Every field line that leaves a closed surface also enters it, because magnetic lines have no beginning or end (no single magnetic poles). So the outward and inward flux cancel and the total is zero.

questions.q: An AVO meter (multimeter) is used to measure:
questions.x: AVO stands for amperes, volts and ohms: the one instrument measures current, potential difference and resistance by switching between ranges.

questions.q: A coil gives an average induced emf ε when the flux through each of its turns changes by ΔΦ in time t. A second coil with twice as many turns has the same change of flux per turn in time t/2. Its average induced emf is:
questions.x: ε = NΔΦ/Δt, so doubling N doubles the emf and halving the time doubles it again: 2 × 2 = 4ε. Counting only one of the two changes gives 2ε.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 60 Ω, XL = 120 Ω and XC = 40 Ω. Its power factor is:
questions.x: Net reactance = 120 − 40 = 80 Ω, so Z = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω and the power factor cos φ = R/Z = 60/100 = 0.6. 0.8 is X/Z (sin φ); 0.5 uses XL alone.

questions.q: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor at room temperature, the number of free electrons in the conduction band compared with the number of holes in the valence band is:
o: Zero, as there are no holes in a pure semiconductor
questions.x: In an intrinsic semiconductor each electron that is thermally excited into the conduction band leaves exactly one hole behind, so the numbers are equal. Unequal numbers of electrons and holes need doping (n-type or p-type).

questions.q: A capacitor of large capacitance is connected in parallel with the load resistor of a full-wave rectifier. The purpose of the capacitor is to:
o: Double the frequency of the output
Smooth the output by charging at the peaks and discharging between them
Block the direct current from reaching the load
Convert the output back into alternating current
questions.x: The capacitor charges to near the peak voltage and then supplies the load while the rectified voltage falls, so the ripple is reduced and the output is nearly steady DC. It does not change the pulse frequency, and in parallel it does not block DC from the load.

questions.q: In a nuclear fission reaction a large amount of energy is released. According to E = mc², this energy comes from:
o: An increase in the total rest mass of the particles
A decrease in the total rest mass of the particles
The kinetic energy of the incoming neutron alone
An increase in the number of protons
questions.x: The total rest mass of the products is less than that of the reactants, and this mass difference Δm appears as energy ΔE = Δm c². The slow incoming neutron brings very little energy, and the number of protons is conserved.

questions.q: An electron starting from rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 150 V. Its de Broglie wavelength is about: (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.x: p = √(2meV) = √(2 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 150) = √(4.37 × 10⁻⁴⁷) ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹, so λ = h/p ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the spacing of atoms in a crystal. Leaving out the 2 in √(2meV) gives 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

questions.q: In Bohr's model the radius of the first orbit of hydrogen is 0.053 nm. The radius of the third orbit (n = 3) is:
questions.x: Bohr radii follow rₙ = n²r₁, so r₃ = 9 × 0.053 = 0.477 nm. Using rₙ = nr₁ gives 0.159 nm; dividing by 3 gives 0.018 nm; using n = 4 gives 0.848 nm.

questions.q: A Geiger-Müller tube detects radiation because the radiation:
o: Ionises the low-pressure gas in the tube, starting an avalanche of ions that gives a pulse of current
Makes the gas glow so brightly that it is seen
Heats the central wire until it melts
Condenses vapour into droplets along its path
questions.x: An entering particle ionises the gas; the high voltage accelerates the freed electrons, which ionise more atoms (an avalanche), and the resulting pulse is counted. Droplets along the path are how a cloud chamber shows tracks.

questions.q: Which fundamental force has an unlimited range and is always attractive?
questions.x: Gravity acts over unlimited distances and only attracts. The electromagnetic force also has unlimited range, but it can attract or repel; the strong and weak forces act only over nuclear distances.

questions.q: An oxide of iron contains 70% iron by mass. Its empirical formula is: (O = 16, Fe = 56)
questions.x: Fe : O = 70/56 : 30/16 = 1.25 : 1.875 = 1 : 1.5 = 2 : 3, so Fe₂O₃ (check: 112/160 = 70%). FeO would be 77.8% Fe and Fe₃O₄ 72.4% Fe; stopping at the ratio 1 : 1.5 without making whole numbers is the common slip.

questions.q: When a paper chromatogram is set up, the base line carrying the spots must be above the level of the solvent in the jar. Otherwise:
o: The solvent would not rise up the paper at all
The Rf values of all spots would become 1
The spots would move faster and give larger Rf values
The spots would dissolve into the solvent in the jar instead of moving up the paper
questions.x: If the spots dip into the solvent, the substances wash out into the solvent in the jar and no chromatogram forms. The solvent still rises by capillary action whatever its level.

questions.q: At what temperature will 2 mol of an ideal gas in a 16.42 dm³ vessel exert a pressure of 3 atm? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.x: T = PV/nR = (3 × 16.42)/(2 × 0.0821) = 300 K = 27 °C. Forgetting n = 2 gives 600 K (327 °C); leaving 300 as °C or adding 273 the wrong way gives the other values.

questions.q: Which compound cannot form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules, but can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules?
questions.x: Propanone has no H on O or N, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, but the lone pairs on its C=O oxygen accept hydrogen bonds from water. Methanol and ammonia hydrogen-bond with themselves; methane can do neither.

questions.q: The ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
questions.x: A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell with 4s¹ is more stable than 3d⁴ 4s², so chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, with six unpaired electrons. Filling strictly by the Aufbau order gives the tempting 3d⁴ 4s².

questions.q: According to Bohr's model, the angular momentum (mvr) of an electron in an allowed orbit is equal to:
questions.x: Bohr's postulate: mvr = nh/2π, where n = 1, 2, 3 … so angular momentum is quantised in units of h/2π.

questions.q: Which diatomic species of period 2 has a bond order of zero according to molecular orbital theory?
questions.x: Be₂ has 4 valence electrons in σ2s² and σ*2s², so bond order = ½(2 − 2) = 0 and the molecule is not stable. Li₂ (σ2s²) has bond order 1, B₂ has 1 and C₂ has 2. Li₂ is tempting because lithium is a metal, but in the gas Li₂ does exist.

questions.q: A gas expands by 2.0 dm³ against a constant external pressure of 100 kPa. How much work does the gas do on its surroundings? (1 kPa dm³ = 1 J)
questions.x: Work = PΔV = 100 kPa × 2.0 dm³ = 200 kPa dm³ = 200 J. Converting 100 kPa to 10⁵ Pa but leaving the volume in dm³ gives 2 × 10⁵, i.e. the 200 kJ slip.

questions.q: Steam reacts with hot coke: C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g). At constant temperature, the pressure on the equilibrium mixture is increased. Which way does the equilibrium shift?
o: To the right, because there are 2 mol of reactants and 2 mol of products
It does not shift, because the total number of moles is equal on both sides
To the left, because there is 1 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right
To the right, because higher pressure always increases the yield
questions.x: Only gas molecules count: 1 mol (H₂O) on the left and 2 mol (CO + H₂) on the right. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, so the equilibrium shifts to the left. Counting the solid carbon makes both sides look equal, the tempting slip.

questions.q: In the nitrating mixture, concentrated sulphuric and nitric acids react: H₂SO₄ + HNO₃ → HSO₄⁻ + H₂NO₃⁺. In this reaction, nitric acid acts as:
questions.x: H₂SO₄, the stronger acid, donates a proton to HNO₃, forming HSO₄⁻ and H₂NO₃⁺ (which then loses water to give NO₂⁺). The proton acceptor, HNO₃, is a Brønsted–Lowry base here. Calling it an acid follows its name, but whether a species acts as acid or base depends on its partner.

questions.q: Which of these 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solutions has the highest pH? (Ka of CH₃COOH = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵; Ka of HCO₃⁻ = 4.7 × 10⁻¹¹)
questions.x: NH₄Cl is acidic and NaCl neutral. Both CO₃²⁻ and CH₃COO⁻ hydrolyse to give OH⁻, but the weaker the parent acid, the stronger its conjugate base: HCO₃⁻ is far weaker than CH₃COOH, so CO₃²⁻ is the stronger base and Na₂CO₃ gives the higher pH. CH₃COONa is tempting because it is the textbook example of a basic salt.

questions.q: Benzene and toluene form a nearly ideal solution; at a given temperature pure benzene has the higher vapour pressure. Compared with the liquid mixture, the vapour in equilibrium with it is:
questions.x: Mole fraction of benzene in the vapour = x(benzene) × p°(benzene)/P, and p°(benzene) is greater than the total pressure P, so the vapour is richer in the more volatile benzene. It is not pure benzene, because toluene also has a vapour pressure.

questions.q: In a zinc–carbon dry cell, manganese dioxide is packed around the central carbon rod. Its main role is to:
o: Act as the anode, which is oxidised
Supply the ions that carry the current through the paste
Act as the oxidising agent reduced at the cathode, so that hydrogen gas does not collect there
Catalyse the oxidation of the zinc case
questions.x: MnO₂ is reduced at the carbon cathode (it is the depolariser), taking up the electrons that would otherwise form hydrogen and stop the cell. The zinc case is the anode, and the NH₄Cl/ZnCl₂ paste is the electrolyte.

questions.q: Threshold energy is the minimum energy colliding molecules must have for a reaction to occur. The activation energy is equal to:
o: Threshold energy + average energy of the reactant molecules
Threshold energy × average energy of the reactant molecules
Average energy of the product molecules − threshold energy
Threshold energy − average energy of the reactant molecules
questions.x: Activation energy is the extra energy reactant molecules need above their average energy to reach the threshold: Ea = threshold energy − average energy of the reactants.

questions.q: The first ionisation energy of nitrogen (1402 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of oxygen (1314 kJ mol⁻¹). The main reason is that:
o: Oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge than nitrogen
Oxygen's outer electron is in a higher shell than nitrogen's
Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p subshell, while in oxygen one 2p orbital holds a pair of electrons that repel each other
Nitrogen atoms are smaller than oxygen atoms
questions.x: In O (2p⁴) the fourth p electron pairs up in one orbital; the repulsion makes it easier to remove, so the general rise across the period is broken. Oxygen actually has the larger nuclear charge and the smaller atom, and both outer electrons are in shell 2.

questions.q: Alkaline earth metals are harder and have higher melting points than the alkali metals of the same period. The main reason is that:
o: Each atom gives two electrons to the sea of electrons, so the metallic bonding is stronger
Their atoms are joined by covalent bonds
questions.x: Group 2 atoms release two valence electrons each and form smaller, doubly charged cations, so the metallic bonding is stronger. Their atoms are smaller and their ionisation energies are higher than those of Group 1.

questions.q: Which of the following double salts is NOT an alum?
questions.x: Alums have the general formula M₂SO₄·M'₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O, with a univalent and a trivalent cation (chrome alum, ferric alum and soda alum all fit). Mohr's salt, FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O, contains Fe²⁺ and only 6 waters, so it is a double salt but not an alum; ferric alum is tempting because it also contains iron.

questions.q: 6.35 g of copper reacts completely with hot concentrated nitric acid. What volume of gas, measured at STP, is given off? (Cu = 63.5; molar volume 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: Concentrated acid gives NO₂: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O. 0.10 mol Cu gives 0.20 mol NO₂ = 4.48 dm³. Using the dilute-acid equation (2 mol NO per 3 mol Cu) gives 1.49 dm³, the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: At room temperature and pressure, chlorine is a:
o: Pale yellow gas that attacks glass
questions.x: Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas. Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey-black solid; the pale yellow gas (fluorine) is the closest mix-up.

questions.q: Aqueous [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ looks purple. The light it mainly absorbs, promoting its single d electron, lies in which region of the visible spectrum?
questions.x: The colour seen is made of the light that is not absorbed; Ti³⁺ absorbs in the yellow-green middle of the spectrum and transmits red and blue, which together look purple. Choosing purple confuses the colour seen with the colour absorbed.

questions.q: Catalytic cracking of heavy petroleum fractions is usually carried out at about 500 °C over:
questions.x: Catalytic cracking uses a silica–alumina (zeolite) catalyst, which allows large molecules to be broken at a lower temperature and pressure than thermal cracking. Nickel is a hydrogenation catalyst, and V₂O₅ and promoted iron belong to the contact and Haber processes.

questions.q: Iodoethane, CH₃CH₂I, is reduced with zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid. The organic product is:
questions.x: Zn/HCl supplies hydrogen that replaces the iodine: CH₃CH₂I + 2[H] → CH₃CH₃ + HI. Butane is the Wurtz product with sodium, and ethene would need elimination with alcoholic KOH.

questions.q: In Friedel–Crafts reactions the aluminium chloride must be anhydrous because:
o: Water reacts with AlCl₃, so it can no longer act as a Lewis acid to form the electrophile
Water reacts with benzene to form phenol
Only anhydrous AlCl₃ can act as an oxidising agent towards benzene
Water changes the product from substitution to addition
questions.x: AlCl₃ works by accepting a lone pair from the halogen of R–Cl or RCO–Cl. Water hydrolyses it (and also gives up a lone pair to it), so no carbocation or acylium ion forms. Benzene does not react with water.

questions.q: The correct IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br is:
questions.x: The longest chain is three carbons (CH₂Br–C–CH₃) with two methyls on C2. Numbering from the CH₂Br end gives the locants 1,2,2; from the other end they are 2,2,3, so the first set wins and 3-bromo is wrong. The butane names belong to isomers with a different skeleton.

questions.q: Excess ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. What is the greatest mass of ethoxyethane that 9.2 g of ethanol can give? (C₂H₅OH = 46, C₂H₅OC₂H₅ = 74 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 9.2/46 = 0.20 mol ethanol; two molecules form one ether molecule, so 0.10 mol × 74 = 7.4 g. Ignoring the 2:1 ratio gives 14.8 g; 9.2 g assumes mass is unchanged and forgets the water lost.

questions.q: Ethanal is warmed with Tollens' reagent and a silver mirror forms. The organic product in the alkaline ammoniacal solution is:
questions.x: Tollens' reagent is a mild oxidising agent: CH₃CHO is oxidised to CH₃COO⁻ while [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is reduced to Ag. Ethanol would be a reduction product, the opposite of what happens.

questions.q: A 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solution of a monobasic carboxylic acid has Ka = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³. Its pH is about (log 2 = 0.30):
questions.x: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) = √(1.6 × 10⁻⁵) = 4 × 10⁻³, so pH = 3 − log 4 = 3 − 0.60 = 2.4. Treating it as a strong acid gives 1.0; forgetting the square root gives 4.8, and 3.8 is pKa.

questions.q: Which alcohol, heated under reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, gives butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
questions.x: A ketone comes from a secondary alcohol with the OH on the same carbon as the C=O, so butanone comes from butan-2-ol. Butan-1-ol would give butanal and then butanoic acid; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary and is not oxidised.

questions.q: Bakelite, a hard thermosetting plastic, is made by condensation polymerisation of phenol with:
questions.x: Phenol and methanal (formaldehyde) join through –CH₂– bridges with loss of water, building a cross-linked network. Ethane-1,2-diol and hexane-1,6-diamine are monomers of polyesters and nylons.

questions.q: Bagasse, used in Pakistan as a raw material for paper and board, is a waste product of the:
questions.x: Bagasse is the fibrous residue left after the juice has been pressed out of sugarcane, so it is a cheap source of cellulose fibre. The other industries do not produce plant fibre waste.

questions.q: In the octal number (5372)₈, what is the decimal value of the digit 3 in its place?
questions.x: From the right the places are 8⁰ = 1, 8¹ = 8, 8² = 64, 8³ = 512; the 3 is in the 64s place, so it is worth 3 × 64 = 192. 24 would be 3 × 8, the next place to the right.

questions.q: A program is written in the machine language of one type of processor. What usually happens if it is moved to a computer whose processor has a different instruction set?
o: It will not run there without being rewritten for that processor
It runs there unchanged, because machine language is the same on all computers
It runs there after it is passed through a compiler once more
It runs there only if the second computer has more memory
questions.x: Machine language is machine-dependent: its binary codes are the instructions of one processor family, so another instruction set will not understand them. A compiler translates high-level source code, not machine code, so recompiling the machine-code program does not help.

questions.q: What is (9A)₁₆ + (27)₁₆?
questions.x: A + 7 = 10 + 7 = 17 = 16 + 1, so write 1 and carry 1; then 9 + 2 + 1 = 12 = C, giving (C1)₁₆. Check in decimal: 154 + 39 = 193 = 12×16 + 1; (B1)₁₆ forgets the carry.

questions.q: Bilal sends an e-mail and adds his CV as a PDF file that travels with the message. The PDF file is called an:
questions.x: A file sent along with an e-mail message is an attachment. The inbox is the folder where received messages are kept.

questions.q: Data is sent as one continuous block of characters, and the sender and receiver are kept in step by timing signals, with no start and stop bits around each character. This is:
questions.x: In synchronous transmission both sides share timing, so blocks of data flow without start and stop bits for each character. Asynchronous transmission is the kind that frames every character with a start bit and a stop bit.

questions.q: In a star network of 6 computers with a hub at the centre, computer P sends a message to computer Q. Which computers receive the signal?
o: Only Q, because the hub reads Q's MAC address
Only P and Q, because the others are switched off by the hub
None, because a hub cannot forward any data
All the other five computers, but only Q keeps the message
questions.x: A hub works at the Physical layer and copies every signal out of all its other ports, so all five receive it; the NICs of the other four see it is not for them and ignore it. Sending only to Q is what a switch does.

questions.q: In computing, bias means that a system:
o: Gives results that are unfair to certain groups of people
Fails to start because of a hardware fault
Copies itself from one file to another
Uses more memory than it needs
questions.x: Bias in computing is when a system's outputs consistently favour or harm some groups, often because of its data or design. Copying itself between files describes a virus, not bias.

questions.q: Sana's antivirus is fully up to date, yet she types her bank password into a fake website after clicking a link in a phishing e-mail. Why did the antivirus not prevent this?
o: Antivirus software works only when the computer is offline
Phishing tricks the user into giving data, so no harmful program needs to run
Phishing e-mails can be read only after they are decrypted
An updated antivirus deletes every e-mail that has a link
questions.x: Phishing is a trick played on the person: Sana typed her password herself, so there was no virus for the antivirus to find. Antivirus also works online and does not delete every e-mail with a link.

questions.q: A company's computer calculates every employee's monthly salary, subtracts tax and other deductions and prints the pay slips. This application is a:
questions.x: A payroll system works out wages, deductions and pay slips for staff. A point-of-sale system handles sales at a shop counter.

questions.q: A1 to A4 hold 3, 5, 2 and 6. B1 holds `=SUM($A$1:A1)` and is filled down to B4. What does B4 show?
questions.x: Filling down keeps `$A$1` fixed and changes `A1` to `A4`, so B4 holds `=SUM($A$1:A4)` = 3 + 5 + 2 + 6 = 16, a running total. 6 would come from adding only A4.

questions.q: A1, A2 and A3 hold 4, 6 and 8, and C1 holds 5. What does `=SUM(A1:A3,C1)` show?
questions.x: The comma lets `SUM` add a range and another cell: 4 + 6 + 8 = 18, plus 5 gives 23. 18 leaves out C1.

questions.q: After Windows starts, the main screen area that shows icons, the background picture and the taskbar is called the:
questions.x: The desktop is the main working screen of Windows, holding icons and the taskbar. The Control Panel and Recycle Bin are tools opened from it.

questions.q: A DBMS keeps the names, data types and sizes of all fields and the tables they belong to, that is, data about the data. Where is this kept?
questions.x: The data dictionary (catalogue) stores metadata, the description of the database's structure. A transaction file holds recent changes to data, not descriptions of the fields.

questions.q: A shop's file holds each customer's name, address and current balance. It is kept permanently and brought up to date from time to time. What type of file is it?
questions.x: A master file holds the main, permanent data of a system, such as customers' balances, and is updated from time to time. A transaction file holds only recent changes, such as one day's sales.

questions.q: A field stores each school's website address so that clicking the value opens the site in a browser. Which data type is meant for this?
questions.x: A Hyperlink field stores an address that opens when it is clicked. Short Text could store the address as plain characters, but clicking it would not open the site.

questions.q: Customers and Orders are joined one-to-many on CustomerID (a Number field), with referential integrity enforced and "Cascade Update Related Fields" ticked. Customer 7 has four orders. The user changes this customer's CustomerID from 7 to 70. What happens?
o: Access refuses the change because orders exist
The four orders change to CustomerID 70 automatically
The four orders keep CustomerID 7 and lose their link
questions.x: Cascade Update copies a change of the primary key to every matching foreign key, so all four orders now show 70. Without the cascade option, Access would refuse the change while related orders exist.

questions.q: Which match of a stage with what it produces is WRONG?
questions.x: The loader produces no file: it copies the executable into main memory to run it. The preprocessor expands the source, the compiler makes object code, and the linker builds the executable.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", (2 + 3) * 4 % 7);
```
questions.x: The brackets come first: 5; then * and %, which have equal precedence, go left to right: 5 * 4 = 20, 20 % 7 = 6. Without the brackets, 2 + 12 % 7 would give 7.

questions.q: Two `case` labels in the same `switch` statement both have the value `3`. What happens?
o: Only the first `case 3` is ever used
Both `case 3` blocks run, one after the other
questions.x: Every case label in one switch must have a different constant value; a repeated value is a compile-time error, so the program does not run at all. C does not quietly pick the first one.
250 is not <= 100 and not <= 200, so the last branch runs: 1300 + (250 - 200) * 10 = 1300 + 500 = 1800. 2500 charges all 250 units at 10, which the ladder does not do.
The loop counts the values of d from 1 to 12 that divide 12 exactly: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, so c = 6. 4 leaves out 1 and 12 themselves, which the test d <= n includes.

questions.q:
This Python code should print the largest number in the list. What does it print, and what is wrong?
```
nums = [-4, -9, -2]
big = 0
for n in nums:
    if n > big:
        big = n
print(big)
```
o: It prints -2; the code is correct
It prints -9; the comparison is the wrong way round
It prints 0; a logic error, because `big` should start at `nums[0]`
It stops with a runtime error at `n > big`
questions.x: Every number in the list is negative, so n > big (n > 0) is never true and big stays 0, which is not even in the list. The program runs without any error message, so this is a logic error; starting with big = nums[0] gives the correct -2.

questions.q: A team copies its source code to a separate server at the end of every day. Which project risk does this mainly reduce?
o: A skilled team member leaving the project
The project going over its budget
Losing work if a developer's computer fails
questions.x: A daily backup on another machine means a crashed or stolen computer costs at most one day of work. It does nothing about changing requirements, staff leaving or cost overruns, which need other risk plans.
The same call `pet.speak()` runs each object's own method (polymorphism): Quack, Meow, Quack. `[0]` takes the first letter of each, printed together: QMQ.

questions.q: A function is defined as `def area(r):` and returns `3 * r * r`. What happens when the program calls `area(2, 3)`?
o: a TypeError, because `area` takes one argument but two are given
questions.x: The number of arguments must match the parameters: `area` has one parameter, so passing two raises a TypeError. Python does not silently ignore an extra argument.

questions.q: What is the index of the first element of a Python list?
o: It depends on the list's length
questions.x: Python lists are indexed from 0, so `L[0]` is the first element. Index −1 is the last element, counting from the end.

questions.q:
For a large `n`, what is the time complexity of this code?
```
for i in range(n):
    print(i)
for j in range(10):
    print(j)
```
questions.x: The first loop runs n times and the second a fixed 10 times, one after the other, so the work is n + 10 steps, which grows like O(n). The loops are not nested, so it is not O(n²).

questions.q: The Undo feature of a text editor undoes the most recent change first. Which data structure suits it best?
questions.x: The last change made is the first one undone, which is last in, first out: a stack. A queue would undo the oldest change first.

questions.q: Binary search, with middle index = (low + high) // 2, is wrongly used on the unsorted list `[9, 2, 7, 4, 5]` to look for 2. What is the result?
o: It reports 2 as not found, although 2 is in the list
It finds 2 after checking every element
It sorts the list first and then finds 2
questions.x: mid = 2 (7): 2 < 7, so high = 1. mid = 0 (9): 2 < 9, so high = −1, and low > high ends the search. Index 1 is never checked, so the search fails; binary search does not sort the list itself.

questions.q: Which chart best compares the number of students enrolled in five different departments of a college?
questions.x: A bar chart compares amounts across separate categories such as departments. A line chart suits change over time, and a histogram shows how a numeric variable is spread over ranges.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
o: A Road Full of New Signs
questions.x: The passage centres on Akram, and the narrator concludes that "Forty people had slept safely because one man stayed awake and paid attention". The road signs and the cotton fields are small details.

questions.q: According to the passage, why did Akram distrust the new road signs?
o: They were too dim to read in the dark
They had been put up in the wrong places
They showed how the road ought to be, not how it was that night
They distracted drivers from watching for cattle
questions.x: Akram says the signs "tell you what the road should be, ... not what it is tonight". He does not say they are dim: the passage calls them "bright new road signs".

questions.q: The passage suggests that most of the passengers did not know that:
o: the driver had skilfully avoided a dangerous truck
the bus had arrived in Multan late
the narrator had been given the driver's seat
the bus had taken a different road from usual
questions.x: Akram passed the truck "so smoothly that most of the passengers never woke", and at Multan "Hardly anyone looked back at the driver". Nothing in the passage says the bus was late or changed its road.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "loomed" most nearly means:
o: appeared suddenly as a large, threatening shape
questions.x: A truck "without tail-lights loomed out of the dark": it rose up suddenly, big and dangerous. Weaving on a frame belongs to the noun "loom", and nothing in the sentence suggests flashing lights.

questions.q: By the end of the passage, the narrator's attitude towards Akram is best described as:
o: mild annoyance at his long silence
grateful respect for his quiet skill
pity for the tiring job he does
questions.x: The narrator credits Akram with the safety of forty people and is the one passenger who looks back, sharing a sign "as if we had shared a secret". Annoyance belongs only to the first hour, when he "assumed" Akram resented him.

questions.q: Which title best fits the passage?
o: Why Meat Rots Faster in Open Jars
How a Fair Comparison Overturned an Old Belief
The Life Cycle of the Common Fly
How New Instruments Changed Early Science
questions.x: The passage tells how the jar test disproved the belief that "rotting meat produced worms" and praises "its comparison". It is not about instruments: the method "does not depend on clever instruments".

questions.q: Why did the experimenter cover some jars with fine cloth in his second test?
o: To keep the meat from rotting too quickly
To answer the objection that sealed jars had kept out air
To let flies reach the meat more easily
To stop mice from getting into the jars
questions.x: Critics said sealing "had shut out the fresh air that life required", so the cloth "let air in but kept flies out". It did not help flies reach the meat; it kept them away from it.

questions.q: The passage suggests that people who believed meat produced maggots went wrong mainly because they:
o: did not care about observing things carefully
had studied only meat and never looked at grain
refused to repeat any test that gave a surprising result
could not watch closely enough to see where the maggots came from
questions.x: They "had no way of watching every fly that landed", and the experiment showed that flies lay eggs where they land. They were not careless: the passage calls them "careful observers".

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "discipline" most nearly means:
o: a branch of study such as biology
self-control in keeping to a careful method
questions.x: "The discipline to change one thing at a time" means the self-control to keep strictly to a method. Punishment is a common meaning of the word, and a branch of study is another, but neither fits "the discipline to change".

questions.q: In the third paragraph, the phrase "that single change" refers to:
o: the change that took place in the meat as it rotted
the critics' change of opinion about the test
the move from glass jars to cloth bags
the one way in which the jars were treated differently
questions.x: The sentence says "Every jar was treated alike except in one respect", and "that single change" is that one respect, such as open versus covered. The rotting happened in every jar, so it was not the difference being tested.
